content.thinking:
I'm going through the claims one by one, starting with the root cause: the typical-purchase feature runs a helper that finds a middle price, which I'm treating as unverified since I haven't actually run the code. The slowdown shows up for shoppers with long histories while most shoppers stay fast, and I'm checking that against the p50 numbers.

I'm checking the rest of the claims against the series data: the slowdown is in the p99 tail while the baseline stayed steady, and the alert itself was built on that tail. Error rates on the account page stayed normal and peaked before the onset, so failures don't explain it. The switch to the flag at 14:15:47 lines up with the first slow requests, and every evaluation before that came back off.

I'm checking the flag switch against the evaluation data: it went from every evaluation off to every evaluation on within the switch minute, which fits an immediate full cutover with no staged rollout or automatic guard showing in the record. I'm also noting that no test or check run appears in the record, and that the only other flag change in the hour before came from someone other than the investigating agent.

I'm checking whether the "nobody was paged" finding holds up: the record shows no on-call incident linked, though Argus did post in Slack, which informs people without bringing anyone in. I'll count that as supported and keep it as its own finding rather than drop it.

I'm verifying the last part of the account-page finding against the record, and it fits what's already been checked.

supported.quote: With typical-purchase-feature on, render_spend_summary calls typical_spend_per_item (src/io_shop/typical_spend.py).
That function finds the middle price by removing the smallest remaining price over and over until it reaches the middle, and each min and each remove is a full pass over the list.
Its work therefore grows far faster than the length of a shopper's purchase history, so requests for shoppers with long histories became very slow while requests for most shoppers stayed fast.
It rests on F1, a reading of the source nothing ran, so it is unverified.

Switching on a new shop feature sent shoppers' pages through a calculation of their typical spend that likely does far more work the more purchases a shopper has made, so pages for shoppers with long purchase histories became very slow.
If typical-purchase-feature is switched back on before a fix is in place, the slowest shop requests could slow down again in the same way.
The slowest shop page loads slowed sharply for some shoppers
Shoppers' slowest requests took much longer to load.
The alert fired on the slowest tail of request durations across the service's replicas, and the Investigator placed the start at the onset.
Failed requests did not rise: the account page error rate stayed within its usual range and peaked before the onset.
Requests began running the code path behind typical-purchase-feature. Admin switched the flag on at {P1.1}.
Before that, every flag evaluation logged came back off. In the minute of the switch the evaluations were mixed, and from the onset on, every evaluation logged came back on.
Any other flag change: the flag provider's history for the hour before showed no flag change by anyone but Argus other than this one.

With the flag on, the account page's spend summary calls a typical-spend calculation whose work, by Code-Fix's reading, grows far faster than the length of a shopper's purchase history, so shoppers with long histories waited much longer.
The flag went straight from off for every evaluation to on for every evaluation.
No staged rollout to a small share of shoppers was seen, and no automatic guard that turns a just-changed flag off when latency rises was seen.
a latency guard could have turned the flag off without waiting for the alert and an agent's action.
No test or check of how the flagged code path performs with long purchase histories was seen before the flag was switched on in production.
Nobody was paged: the alert was not linked to any on-call incident, so no person was brought in while the incident ran.
rows: Nobody was paged: no on-call incident was linked to this one.
